- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.75) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to sentiment-driven momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward correction — instead, allow a slight lagged rebound (e.g., +2–3% below forecast) to reflect sentiment’s delayed impact.
- In cases of sustained upward trend in history + strong positive sentiment, model tends to overestimate later peaks — apply mean reversion correction by subtracting 1–2% from forecasted peak values after 10+ consecutive days of rising prices.
- When sentiment is mixed or volatile (±0.3–0.7), forecast should be smoothed — reduce volatility by averaging 3–5 consecutive forecast points to avoid overfitting to short-term sentiment swings.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion after a spike (e.g., 3–5 days of high prices followed by drop), reduce forecasted peak by 5–10% and shift mean reversion window to 7–10 days for better alignment with sentiment decay.
- For horizon > 14 days, sentiment should be weighted more heavily in correction — if sentiment is positive, add 1–2% to forecast; if negative, subtract 1–2% to avoid overconfidence in sentiment-driven trends.
